name: Sunbathing / tanmaxxing

lead: Tanmaxxing means darkening the skin with sunbathing, tanning lotions, lamps or sunless products for a warmer, healthier-looking complexion. Tanned skin has been fashionable in the West since the 1920s, and looksmaxxing guides treat colour as part of skin and overall appearance.

UV radiation prompts melanocytes to make melanin. UVA darkens existing pigment, while UVB causes DNA damage that triggers new melanin and a tan that appears a few days later. Sunless self-tanners using dihydroxyacetone react with proteins in the outer skin layer to produce a brown colour without UV.

paras: People get gradual sun exposure, use tanning lotions or oils, visit tanning beds, or apply sunless self-tanner, which gives colour within hours. UV tans build over days to weeks. Sun exposure also supports vitamin D production.

Excess UV is associated with sunburn, DNA mutations, skin cancer, accelerated skin ageing and immune suppression. A 2010 study linked frequent tanning bed use to about triple the melanoma risk. The WHO, American Cancer Society and US Surgeon General warn against excessive sun and indoor tanning. Fair skin burns more easily.

angle.text: Tanmaxxing darkens the skin with sun, lamps, lotions or sunless products for a warmer, healthier-looking complexion, and the colour change shows right away. Tanning is the skin's pigment response to UV; sunless products based on dihydroxyacetone give colour without UV.

lead: Tanmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for darkening the skin, by sunbathing, tanning oils and lotions, tanning devices or sunless products, to look healthier, warmer in tone and more defined. Tanning itself is the skin's pigment response to ultraviolet radiation.[1] People pursue it because colour is a visible part of overall presentation: a tan is a visible change in skin tone that has been a fashion signal since the 1920s, and guides present it as part of skin and overall presentation.[1][2]

Looksmaxxing guides describe sun tanning as the basic method, supplemented by tanning oils and lotions, and by sunless options such as dihydroxyacetone (DHA) self-tanners that darken skin without UV.[2][1] Sun exposure also supports vitamin D production.[1]

The appearance chain is direct and visible: UV exposure or a sunless product darkens the skin within hours to days, which evens out tone, adds warmth and can make facial contours and muscle definition read more clearly in photos. How much colour a person can build depends on skin type, which dermatologists describe with the Fitzpatrick scale.[3][1]

Research and public-health bodies document that UV exposure is associated with sunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer. The WHO, the American Cancer Society and the US Surgeon General warn against excessive sun and indoor tanning exposure, and the WHO says sunbeds should never be used to obtain vitamin D.[1][4][5]
infobox: DHA self-tanners; colour fades in about 3 to 10 days[18]

paras: Before the 1920s in the US and Western Europe, tanned skin signalled outdoor labour and lower class, and upper classes used parasols and covering clothing. Sunlight was promoted as therapy in the early 1900s; Niels Finsen received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Medicine for light therapy.[1] Tans became fashionable in the 1920s, with Coco Chanel's Riviera tan widely imitated, and Jean Patou launched the first sun tan oil in 1927.[1] SPF ratings began in 1962, and tanning beds appeared from 1978.[1]

Indoor tanning devices emit artificial UV, mostly UVA with a small share of UVB from low-pressure fluorescent tubes; US maximum session times are set by manufacturers from the time needed to reach four minimal erythema doses.[6] The FDA, citing the Indoor Tanning Association, reported about 25,000 US salons in 2010 and about 30 million visitors a year; salon numbers later fell by roughly 30 percent between 2008 and 2015, and a 10 percent federal excise tax on tanning services took effect in 2010.[6]

Melanocytes produce melanin, either red pheomelanin or dark brown eumelanin. UVA darkens existing melanin quickly through oxidative stress and fades, while UVB causes direct DNA damage that triggers new melanin production, yielding a tan after two to three days that offers modest protection, roughly equivalent to SPF 3. The Fitzpatrick scale from 1975 classifies skin types I to VI by burning and tanning tendency.[1]

Melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis make melanin and pass it to surrounding keratinocytes. Humans have broadly similar numbers of melanocytes across skin tones; differences in colour come from how much and what kind of melanin they produce. Dark brown-black eumelanin absorbs UV and is thought to protect skin cell DNA, while red-yellow pheomelanin absorbs less and may add to UV damage; higher melanin content correlates with lower skin cancer incidence.[7]

The Fitzpatrick scale, created in 1975 by dermatologist Thomas B. Fitzpatrick to set UVA doses for PUVA therapy, classifies skin into six types by how it burns and tans: type I always burns and never tans, type II usually burns and tans minimally, type III sometimes burns and tans evenly, type IV burns minimally and always tans, type V very rarely burns, and type VI never burns.[3] Critics note it was built around white skin, relies on self-report, and has been found inadequate even for sorting some European samples.[3]
This is why community guides open by saying that some people tan quickly, some hardly at all, and some turn red and uneven.[2] The scale gives a vocabulary for that variation.

A reference source lists moderate sun exposure as supporting vitamin D synthesis, and excess UV as causing sunburn, DNA mutations, skin cancer, photoaging and immune suppression.[1] A 2024 expert review states that in fair-skinned populations up to 95 percent of keratinocyte skin cancers and 70 to 95 percent of cutaneous melanomas are caused by ultraviolet radiation.[4] Photodamage begins early in childhood, with 50 to 80 percent of lifetime UV exposure occurring before age 18, according to a 1999 review.[8]

A Danish study of sun seekers on a one-week holiday examined sunburn rates during sunbathing.[9] Earlier case-control research found increased melanoma risk with severe sunburn before age 15 and with sunbathing.[10] The sources describe UVA exposure as triggering beta-endorphin release, and a small 2006 trial reported withdrawal-like symptoms in frequent tanners given an opioid blocker.[1]
Guidance summarised in reference sources says to avoid sunburn, to use sunscreen, to recognise that a tan is a response to DNA damage, and to consider sunless alternatives.[1]

SPF, introduced in 1974, expresses the fraction of burning UVB that reaches the skin; the sunscreen reference notes that higher numbers do not last longer and that most people apply less than the tested amount.[11] Broad-spectrum products also address UVA, which penetrates deeper and contributes to DNA damage with little reddening.[11]

Looksmaxxing guides pair tanning with SPF products to colour evenly and avoid burns.[2] Sunscreen reference material reports that sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, that a 2013 Australian study of about 900 adults found smoother skin after 4.5 years of daily broad-spectrum use, and that a small study of 32 people found daily SPF 30 reversed photoaging within 12 weeks.[11] Sunscreen also reduces UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis, though reference sources say typical use does not usually cause deficiency.[11]

A tan itself is described as offering modest protection, roughly SPF 3.[1] Some tanning guides call this a 'base tan' that protects against burning; the Danish holiday study, in which all 25 volunteers burned within a week, and the childhood-exposure review are the research most often raised alongside that idea.[8][9]

The WHO's IARC classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen, citing a 2009 review in The Lancet Oncology.[6] A 2012 analysis found a 20 percent higher melanoma risk among ever-users of tanning devices, rising to 59 percent for those who started before age 35, and a 2014 meta-analysis found 16 percent overall.[6] Wikipedia also reports estimates of about 450,000 non-melanoma skin cancers and more than 10,000 melanomas a year attributable to indoor tanning across the US, Europe and Australia.[6]

Regulation varies. Brazil banned cosmetic use of tanning beds in 2009, the first national ban; commercial tanning services were banned across Australia by 2015; France banned minors in 1997 and many European countries, including the UK, now bar under-18s; in the US, 15 states and the District of Columbia banned use by under-18s as of January 2017, and the FDA moved tanning beds to 'moderate risk' devices in 2014 with a warning against use under 18.[6] The FTC settled with physician Joseph Mercola in 2016 over claims for his tanning beds, with refunds of $5.3 million.[6]

In a study of 25 Danish sun seekers on a one-week Canary Islands holiday, personal UV dosimeters and daily skin exams found that all volunteers sunburned at some point, and sunburn risk correlated with body-site-specific UV dose; the authors concluded that melanin protection was insufficient to prevent sunburn in a week.[9]

An Italian school programme in 1,945 children aged 8-9 gave 1,309 children sun-awareness education, and sunburn fell from 14.6 percent to 10 percent in that group.[12] A study of Italian teenagers examined awareness and risk with sunbathing and sunlamps.[13] Reviews of photoprotection discuss newer approaches beyond sunscreen.[14]

The WHO says small amounts of UV help the body make vitamin D, which supports bones and muscles, and that people with little sun exposure may need supplements.[5] A randomised trial in nursing-home residents examined the effect of sunlight exposure on vitamin D level.[15] Another trial examined how UV protection influences fructosamine after sun exposure in healthy adults.[16]
The WHO estimates that over 1.5 million skin cancers were diagnosed in 2020 and more than 120,000 people died from them, and that UV is linked to around 10 percent of cataract-related blindness.[5]

UVB triggers vitamin D3 synthesis in the epidermis, and one estimate puts skin synthesis at roughly 80 percent of the supply for many people. Latitude, season, age, air pollution, clothing and skin pigmentation all change how much is made; end-of-winter blood levels can be one-third to one-half of end-of-summer levels.[17]

Reference sources note that sunlight alone is unlikely to cause vitamin D toxicity, which is linked to excess supplementation, and that the UK NHS advises year-round supplements for at-risk groups while the WHO notes sunbeds should not be used to obtain vitamin D.[17][5]

Reference sources describe UVA as triggering beta-endorphin release, and a small 2006 trial reported withdrawal-like symptoms in frequent tanners given an opioid blocker.[1] Wikipedia's indoor tanning article notes that excessive tanning causing personal distress is recognised as a psychiatric disorder, sometimes called 'tanorexia' in the media, and that a 2017 Yale paper found evidence of dependence.[6]

Dihydroxyacetone (DHA) is not a dye. It reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard-type reaction, producing brown colour without UV or involvement of underlying pigment. The colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days as the surface skin sheds.[18]

Products include lotions and creams with roughly 3 to 5 percent DHA, sometimes with the slower-developing erythrulose; professional airbrush or booth spray tans lasting about 5 to 10 days; and wash-off bronzers that give temporary colour.[18] Eva Wittgenstein noticed DHA staining skin brown at Cincinnati Children's Hospital in the 1950s, Man-Tan became the first commercial self-tanner in 1959, and Coppertone's Quick Tan followed in 1960; early products were known for orange tones, and from the late 1990s automated spray booths broadened the market.[18]

Safety notes in the reference record: the FDA approved DHA for external use but not around the eyes or mouth or for inhalation, which spray booths can make hard to avoid; DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis; and tanners provide no UV protection themselves.[18] A 2007 study reported more free radicals when DHA-treated skin was exposed to sun, and a 2004 study reported DNA damage in cultured cells; the record also notes criticism of an EU opinion for relying on industry-linked studies.[18] A nationwide survey has profiled users of sunless tanning products.[19]

Oral carotenoid products (beta-carotene, lycopene, canthaxanthin) colour the skin and the colour can last months. The FDA has not approved canthaxanthin for tanning and has issued warnings, with reported effects including hepatitis and retinopathy; the American Cancer Society says beta-carotene pills are not approved for tanning.[18]

Tyrosine-based 'accelerator' lotions and pills are marketed as boosting melanin; the reference record says no scientific data support these claims.[18] Melanotan peptides, sold online and in some gyms, are described in the same record as not legal in any jurisdiction, and health agencies in several countries began warning against them in 2007; this wiki does not give dosing or sourcing for such products.[18]
No studies found testing tanning for attractiveness or looks outcomes. Human studies instead address sunburn behaviour, skin cancer risk, photoaging and vitamin D, as summarised above.[4][9][10]

A looksmax.org guide describes tanning with the sun as the basic method, recommends products such as tanning oils and lotions with SPF, and also covers ways to get colour without the sun.[2] Looksmaxxing guides treat colour as one component of skin and overall presentation.

The guide opens by saying that some people tan fast, some do not tan at all, and some end up red, uneven or fading after two days, and then lists five product types: tanning oils with SPF, lotions, accelerators and sunless options.[2] On looksmax.org, a poster in a thread about sunbathing said they sunbathed each summer after a winter of low mood, a framing that ties sunlight to hormones and wellbeing; other members replied with jokes about Nordic men who need no tan.[20]

lore.intro: Tanmaxxing guides on looksmax.org present tanning, with sun and with products, as part of skin optimisation.[2]
